name: ReclamationConveyanceLines
title: Reclamation Conveyance Lines
description:
This GIS layer represents the spatial alignment and key attributes of conveyance infrastructure—such as canals, pipelines, and tunnels—owned, operated, or managed by the Bureau of Reclamation. It is part of the Enterprise Asset Registry used to support infrastructure asset management, water delivery operations, and planning activities. Each feature in the layer corresponds to a linear conveyance asset and includes associated metadata such as facility name, conveyance type, associated project or system, region, and ownership status. The dataset is maintained by Reclamation’s Asset Management Office and is periodically updated to reflect changes in infrastructure inventory and condition.

Definitions

Canal: A canal is an open channel conveyance feature typically with a trapezoidal cross section. They are constructed with and supported primarily by soil in both cut and fill, depending on the topography which they cross. They may be lined to reduce roughness and seepage. Canals are generally flat and have relatively low velocity. The canal asset type may include natural waterways that are typically associated with the drain functional class, and can include ditches, ephemeral streams, arroyos, and rivers.

Pipe: A pipe is an enclosed structure typically with a circular cross section. They are constructed with many materials but primarily concrete, steel, or plastic and can convey water in both a pressurized and open channel condition. Pipes can also be buried or above ground and are often designed for steeper slopes with higher velocities than canals.

Tunnel: A tunnel is an underground passage constructed by excavating through native earth. They are generally circular but often constructed with a horseshoe cross section. Tunnels can be constructed through soil or rock and require varying amounts of internal support depending on the integrity of the in-situ material through which they pass. Like canals they are often lined to increase hydraulic efficiency. Like pipes, they may have pressurized or open channel flow, and a range of velocities. While tunnels typically convey water directly, they often house internal conduits or pipes to pass liquid, pressurized gas, or wires. For the purpose of the Asset Registry, if a pipe has been constructed within a tunnel as the primary mechanism of water conveyance both the tunnel and pipe should be in the Asset Registry.

Flume: A flume is a constructed waterway which conveys open channel flow. They typically have a square or semicircular cross section and are usually constructed from concrete or steel pipe respectively. Flumes are used to move water across terrain too varied and steep to use a canal or where there is limited right of way. As a result, they are typically benched along a slope or elevated by a supporting structure. Unlike canals, flumes have a self-supporting structural cross section and do not require embankment or native ground for support other than as a foundation. Flow measurement flumes will not be included.
snippet: The objective of the Conveyance Lines Asset Class is to establish a single authoritative source in GIS format for Reclamation's entire inventory of conveyance lines and implement processes and procedures for maintaining the inventory into the future.
